rv.q: If we must have an adaptation, it’s impossible to imagine a better one than this.
This got me in a way that the film didn’t, because the sheer persistent wow factor of the staging makes the story’s strange magic too palpable to resist.
The strange and powerful magic of Miyazaki transcends everything and holds us enrapt in its spell.

There are many other meals in this lavishly imaginative surtitled adaptation from Japan, which is meticulous in its visual detail and choreography, delightful in its puppetry, both meditative and whirling in its speed, and packed full of comedy and adventure.
The show's fidelity to the film is, however, both its attraction and its weakness.
The star of this, the no-face creature (Hikaru Yamano), is a shimmering presence of utter loneliness that gives the show its eerie poetic undertow.
For pure spectacle Spirited Away ... is quite something — thanks to a rotating timber-framed traditional Japanese house buried in a green glade.
Still, when you can list the effects, however striking, something else is not happening: a transformation, a dissolve of one thing into another.
A proper West End spectacle and it is really very cool that a foreign language production is taking up residence in London's biggest theatre for four months.
So if you ask me what Spirited Away is really about, I’d say it’s about an hour too long.
Its slick, efficient delivery and reverence for its origins mean it lacks flesh-and-blood immediacy.

Here, the film’s shimmery sense of wonder has undergone a rather dutiful theatrical solidification – the approach is authentic-feeling in its use of masks and puppets (Toby Olié), yet a whiff of the inorganic persists.
Still, it’s an epic — directed by the Les Mis veteran John Caird — which, despite its intelligent use of traditional Japanese imagery, grinds you into submission.
For those who do, there’s nothing that compares.
As Chihiro faces each new challenge, this is a production that carries you with it.
The care the team has put into every detail is remarkable.
This show is so transfixingly beautiful and so completely assured that it feels like balm; it's almost hypnotically assured.
It’s a materialisation of Miyazaki’s genius more than an adaptation: it’s event theatre at its best.
Although spectacular, the human quest is lost a little and it begins to register a bit flat.
That’s particularly unhelpful in a show which may please its many ardent fans but only rarely generates emotion beyond recognition of how cunningly it reproduces the original.
What’s missing, though, is human connection.
Astonishing, mesmerising, and consistently amazing, Spirited Away really could be the theatre event of the year.
And having witnessed opening night as a Studio Ghibli fan, we can confirm it’s an utterly enchanting experience.
Whether anime fans or not, I promise that you’re in for a treat.
I highly recommend you spirit yourself away to see it.
Rarely a minute passes when something doesn't bring a smile to your face.
Spirited Away is magnificent, beautiful and extremely theatrically clever.
It adds to the sense of a production that has made no compromises in creating some of the most astounding sights you will see on a stage.
Its gorgeous storytelling and awe-inspiring visuals more than make up for it.
It’s an imaginative coming-of-age tale and visually stunning.
But if I found the overall effect a little cold, many individual elements are full of charm, especially in the stagecraft used.

cn.t: Spectacular puppetry and visual effects dazzle in this ambitious adaptation, but the three-hour runtime and cultural distance leave some critics enchanted and others emotionally unmoved despite its technical virtuosity.

vr.q: it is still visually stunning and if you have any kind of relationship to this film I think you're going to have a wonderful time at Spirited Away
I definitely would recommend it as long as you kinda go in knowing what to expect
